newsitem.title: USA: E.W. Scripps annual report enters Dilbert Zone.
newsitem.headline: E.W. Scripps annual report enters Dilbert Zone.

text.p: Dilbert, the popular cartoon critic of corporate culture, has a thing or two to tell E.W. Scripps Co. -- in the media company's 1996 annual report.

In the middle of Chief Executive Officer William Burleigh's letter to shareholders, the plain-talking engineer pops up with a query, "I wonder if this is a clever shift in management philosophy or a simple application of shareowner jargon-spewing?"
Dilbert's pointy-haired, nameless boss stands next to a chart showing a comparison of Scripps' cumulative five-year total return and comments, "Lines going up are good."
On a page of tabular material summarizing results of the company's broadcast television segment, Dilbert and his boss have this exchange, "Boss: Hmmm. It's still a bit too readable."
"Dilbert: I could reduce the type size and run it through the fax."
Elsewhere, Dilbert's dog, Dogbert, smirks, "I saved the company a fortune by sending the headquarters staff on one-way business trips."
United Media, a subsidiary of Cincinnati-based Scripps, syndicates Dilbert to some 1,400 newspapers in 35 countries, reaching a daily readership of 150 million.

Scripps' director of investor relations, Richard Boehne, said pressing Dilbert into the company's service was "a one-time opportunity. The character makes fun of corporate types like us ... so we let him make fun of us."
Reaction to the humorous interloper, Boehne said, has been "overwhelmingly positive."

"How do you make an annual report stand out? It's very difficult," Boehne added. "Dilbert does such a good job of telling us what we all know to be true -- yet we get so mired in corporateness that we forget. (Cartoonist) Scott Adams does a good job of saying what everybody's thinking."
